abstract.t: Merkle Tree Certificates (MTC) replace the signature of a Certification Authority (CA) with smaller inclusion proof against a periodically published landmark. The large sizes of post-quantum (PQC) keys and signatures make conventional certificate chains costly to validate on constrained devices, which have limited memory, compute, and message-size budgets. MTC's lightweight properties keep certificate verification practical for such devices even when PQC signature algorithms are used.

This document specifies how to carry MTC credentials in the Lightweight Authenticated Key Exchange (LAKE) protocol : CBOR encodings of MTC certificates and landmarks, and a new External Authorization Data (EAD) item that lets the two peers negotiate, per message, between the compact landmark-relative form of a certificate and its self-contained standalone form.

section.name: Introduction
section.t: Merkle Tree Certificates (MTC) change the way a Certification Authority (CA) vouches for the certificates it issues. Instead of signing every certificate individually, as in a conventional PKI, an MTC CA appends each certificate it issues to an issuance log, which is a Merkle tree in the style of Certificate Transparency . At regular intervals, the CA designates the current tree size as a landmark and publishes the hashes of the subtrees that cover the log up to that size; a set of cosigners checks that the log has only grown and signs these subtree hashes. A certificate then carries an inclusion proof in the place of the CA signature: the proof lists the sibling hashes along the path from the certificate's leaf up to a subtree root covered by a landmark, and the relying party recomputes this path and compares the result against a landmark it already trusts.

This construction is attractive for devices described in the taxonomy of , because it replaces the CA signature, which grows large with post-quantum signature algorithms such as ML-DSA , with an inclusion proof whose size grows only with the logarithm of the number of certificates in the log. A landmark-relative certificate for a log of a million entries carries about twenty 32-byte hashes, and verifying it costs only a few SHA-256 computations, which even a class 1 device performs quickly.

The Lightweight Authenticated Key Exchange (LAKE) protocol is a lightweight authenticated key exchange protocol designed for constrained devices and networks. This document specifies how to carry MTC credentials in LAKE: how a certificate is encoded, and a new External Authorization Data (EAD) item that lets the two peers negotiate, for each message, whether the compact landmark-relative form of a certificate or its self-contained standalone form is sent. This negotiation lets a device keep presenting the smallest certificate form its peer can verify, without assuming that the peer already holds the same landmarks, while every verifier remains able to fall back to the standalone form that any relying party can check.

section.name: Motivation
section.t: None of the three post-quantum signature algorithms standardized by the US National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) keeps certificate chains within the message sizes and link budgets that LAKE and the networks beneath it are designed for without a trade-off. FN-DSA keeps the smallest signatures of the three, but even its smallest variant remains far larger than the pre-quantum signatures it replaces, and reaching that size requires an implementation that depends on carefully constructed Gaussian sampling, and a flawed implementation can leak the signing key through side channels.

SLH-DSA sits at the opposite end: its security rests only on the properties of its underlying hash function, which makes it the most conservative choice, both from security and implementation perspective, but its signatures run into the tens of kilobytes and its signing is comparatively slow. A conventional PKI must pick one of these trade-offs and pay its cost on every certificate.

MTC decouples this choice from the cost paid by every certificate. Because the CA and cosigners sign a landmark only once per interval rather than once per certificate, this signature cost is amortised across every certificate issued since the previous landmark: the CA and each cosigner can pick whichever algorithm suits their own trade-off between signature size, signing speed, and implementation risk, including a conservative but large scheme such as SLH-DSA , without passing that cost on to every certificate a device presents, which still carries only a small inclusion proof regardless of which algorithm the CA and cosigners chose.

Because every certificate appears in a log that a set of independent cosigners checks, the operator of a device fleet gains a means to detect certificates that were issued without authorisation, a property that a conventional PKI does not provide without additional infrastructure such as Certificate Transparency. MTC addresses only the cost of verifying a peer's certificate. A device's own authentication signature in LAKE still depends on whichever algorithm it holds a key for, with the memory, performance, and side-channel costs that implementation entails . Realising these benefits for devices that authenticate with LAKE requires certificate encodings and a negotiation mechanism that fit within LAKE's credential identifiers and EAD fields.

section.name: Terminology
section.t: The key words "MUST", "MUST NOT", "REQUIRED", "SHALL", "SHALL NOT", "SHOULD", "SHOULD NOT", "RECOMMENDED", "NOT RECOMMENDED", "MAY", and "OPTIONAL" in this document are to be interpreted as described in BCP 14 when, and only when, they appear in all capitals, as shown here.

This document uses the terms defined in , including issuance log, landmark, cosigner, inclusion proof, standalone certificate, and landmark-relative certificate. It also uses the device classes defined in . In addition, this document uses the following terms:

dd.t: A device as characterized in , participating in the LAKE exchange as the party that authenticates with an MTC credential and that keeps a limited cache of landmarks.
An online peer that a constrained device communicates with, and which relays the device's certificate requests and landmark updates to the MTC CA and its cosigners.
The range of landmark numbers, for a given CA, that a party holds in its cache, expressed as the oldest and newest landmark number it has for that CA.
A COSE_Sign1 structure, signed by the CA and countersigned by its cosigners, that communicates one or more new landmarks together with a consistency proof showing that the log has only grown.
The server that a device designates, in delegated mode, to perform the MTC checks on its behalf and to supply it with validated landmarks.
A landmark validation mode in which a device trusts its designated update server to perform the MTC checks on new landmarks, rather than performing them itself.
A landmark validation mode in which a device performs the MTC checks on new landmarks itself, and can accept updates relayed by any peer.
The state a device stores to protect its landmark cache against rollback, consisting of the number, tree size, and root hash of the newest landmark it has validated.

section.name: Design
section.t: This document considers three parties: a constrained device, an online server or gateway with which the device communicates, and an MTC CA that records every certificate it issues in an issuance log checked by a set of independent cosigners. The device and the server authenticate each other with certificates carried in LAKE messages during key establishment. The server relays the device's certificate requests to the CA, stays current with the CA's landmarks, and verifies the device's certificates with hashes rather than signatures.
Solution uses CBOR signed and encoded certificate (). The CA logs the CBOR TBS structure itself, which requires a new issuance log entry type and requires that the CA support it.

section.name: CBOR Encoding of Certificates and Landmarks
section.t: The inclusion proof is a CBOR array containing the index range of the subtree, the inclusion path as a sequence of 32-byte hashes (when SHA-256 is used), and, for the standalone form, the cosignatures over the subtree encoded as COSE_Sign1 signatures . The landmark-relative form omits the cosignatures. Since the certificate type and the algorithm code point already identify an MTC credential, LAKE carries it with the existing credential identifiers, c5c for C509 and x5chain for X.509 , and no new ID_CRED parameter is needed.

A landmark is encoded as a CBOR array containing the CA identifier, the landmark number, the tree size, and the subtree hashes that cover the tree at that size. The CA identifier reuses the trust anchor identifier of the MTC CA , encoded with the CBOR tag for object identifiers . Landmark numbers are consecutive for a given CA identifier, so the pair formed by the CA identifier and the landmark number designates a landmark compactly.

Landmarks reach devices in update packages. An update package is a COSE_Sign1 object in which the CA signs the previous and new tree sizes, the new landmarks, and a consistency proof showing that the new tree size extends the old one, that is each cosigner adds a COSE countersignature . An update package is therefore self-authenticating, and any party may relay it.

section.name: Landmark Negotiation in LAKE
section.t: LAKE lets applications attach data to each of its messages through External Authorization Data (EAD) fields . An EAD field is a sequence of items, each made of an integer label and an optional byte string value, and the sign of the label indicates to the receiver whether the item is critical. This document defines one new item, called landmark state. Its value is a CBOR array that lists, for each CA that the sender trusts, the CA identifier together with the oldest and newest landmark numbers it holds. Because a verifier keeps a contiguous range of landmarks per CA, this range describes its whole cache in a few tens of bytes.

The initiator places its landmark state in EAD_1. The responder compares it with the landmark that covers its own certificate and sends the landmark-relative form in message_2 when the initiator holds that landmark, and the standalone form otherwise. The responder places its own landmark state in EAD_2, and the initiator makes the same choice for message_3. The following diagram summarizes the exchange:

artset.artwork: Initiator (device) Responder (server) | | | message_1: G_X, C_I, EAD_1: landmark state of I | +------------------------------------------------------------------>| | chooses the form of MTC_R | | message_2: G_Y, Enc(C_R, ID_CRED_R: MTC_R, Sig_R, | | EAD_2: landmark state of R, opt. package) | |<------------------------------------------------------------------+ | verifies MTC_R and Sig_R, chooses the form of MTC_I | | message_3: Enc(ID_CRED_I: MTC_I, Sig_I, EAD_3) | +------------------------------------------------------------------>| | verifies MTC_I and Sig_I | | message_4: Enc(EAD_4: update package) | |<------------------------------------------------------------------+ | verifies the package, updates its landmark cache |

section.t: The landmark state item is non-critical: a peer that does not understand it ignores it, and the sender falls back to the standalone form, which every verifier can check. If a verifier nevertheless receives a form it cannot verify, it MUST abort with a LAKE error, and the initiator restarts the exchange with the standalone form. discusses the exposure of the landmark state item across these messages.

section.name: Landmark Synchronisation
section.t: A device that verifies landmark-relative certificates MUST hold, for each CA it trusts, the subtrees of every active landmark. A landmark remains active until every certificate it covers has expired, so a CA that follows the allocation procedure of keeps at most

landmarks active, where T_cert is the maximum certificate lifetime and T_lm is the time between landmarks. Next to its landmarks, a device stores an anchor made of the number of its newest landmark together with the tree size and root hash of the checkpoint against which it last validated its cache; every later update MUST extend this anchor.
How a device validates new landmarks depends on whom it trusts to deliver them. This document defines two validation modes:

dd.t: The device designates one server, typically the enrollment server of the organisation that operates the device, as its update server. This server performs the MTC checks and sends the device only the number, tree size, and subtree hashes of each new landmark, protected by OSCORE or carried in EAD_4 once the server has authenticated.

The device performs the MTC checks itself and can accept updates relayed by any peer. The update package then carries a reference checkpoint at least as large as the newest landmark, a consistency proof from the anchor to the reference checkpoint, and the subtree hashes of each new landmark with a subtree consistency proof towards the reference checkpoint.

section.t: An update proceeds in four steps: (1) the device, or its server, detects that the cache lags behind, either because the landmark state received in EAD_1 or EAD_2 is older than the peer's own, through a CoAP Observe notification on the landmark resource, or on a schedule; (2) the device obtains the update package, either embedded in EAD_4 of message_4 for small increments, or by fetching it from the landmark resource of its designated update server for larger catch-ups; (3) the device verifies the package according to its validation mode; and (4) on success, the device commits the result by writing the new landmarks into free storage, advancing its anchor in a single atomic write, and then releasing the landmarks that have left the active window. A failure at any step leaves the device able to authenticate with standalone certificates, and no failure undoes state the device has already committed.
The anchor also protects the cache against rollback (see ) for the threat model this protects against and for the recovery mode a device enters when that protection fails.

Many constrained devices have no reliable clock, yet landmarks carry an expiration time and certificates carry a validity period. Such a device can still bound the age of a landmark by its number - that is, because the CA allocates at most one landmark per interval, a landmark at least W numbers older than the newest one the device holds has certainly expired and can be discarded. This bound only advances when the device synchronises, and a device that stays offline cannot tell how much time has passed and keeps treating its last landmarks as active.

LAKE does not limit the size of EAD fields, so the practical limit on message size comes from the transport and the link layer. The landmark state item fits in EAD_1 and adds little to message_1. For update packages, landmark hashes contribute only 32 bytes per subtree, but each package carries at least two signatures, from the CA and from one cosigner, and with a post-quantum signature algorithm signatures size dominates the size of the package. Implementations SHOULD deliver large updates through the fetch mechanism described above and reserve EAD_4 for small increments, and MAY batch several landmarks into one update package to amortise the cost of its signatures.

section.name: Exposure of the Landmark State Item
section.t: The protection that LAKE affords to each message differs, and the exposure of the landmark state item defined in differs with it. EAD_1 travels in the clear, so an observer learns which CAs the initiator trusts and how recent its cache is. EAD_2 is encrypted and covered by the responder's authentication, and EAD_3 and EAD_4 are fully protected. An attacker who alters or removes the item in EAD_1 cannot remain unnoticed, because message_1 enters the transcript hash that both peers authenticate; the worst outcome of such interference is a failed exchange or a fallback to the larger standalone form.

section.name: Landmark Cache Rollback Protection
section.t: The anchor described in protects a device's landmark cache against rollback.

dd.t: It is the adversary LAKE is designed to resist. An ordinary non-volatile storage suffices, because the device accepts only packages whose landmark numbers continue from its newest landmark and, in end-to-end mode, whose consistency proof starts at its anchor.

dl.dt: An adversary with physical access or on-device code execution ability:

dd.t: The anchor needs to reside in storage that is authenticated and rollback-resistant, such as a monotonic counter in a secure element, a replay-protected memory block, or one-time-programmable fuses. Many class 1 devices offer none of these, and this document does not assume that they do.

section.t: A device without rollback-resistant storage keeps its anchor in ordinary flash, protected by a message authentication code under a device key. If the anchor is missing or fails this check, the device MUST clear its landmark cache, accept only standalone certificates, and announce no landmark state. It leaves this recovery mode with the first package that passes end-to-end verification against the cosigner keys provisioned at manufacture, or with an update from its designated server in delegated mode, adopting the reference checkpoint of that package as its new anchor.

abstract.t: This document specifies Ephemeral Diffie-Hellman Over COSE (EDHOC), a very compact and lightweight authenticated Diffie-Hellman key exchange with ephemeral keys. EDHOC provides mutual authentication, forward secrecy, and identity protection. EDHOC is intended for usage in constrained scenarios, and a main use case is to establish an Object Security for Constrained RESTful Environments (OSCORE) security context. By reusing CBOR Object Signing and Encryption (COSE) for cryptography, Concise Binary Object Representation (CBOR) for encoding, and Constrained Application Protocol (CoAP) for transport, the additional code size can be kept very low.

front.title: Key words for use in RFCs to Indicate Requirement Levels

abstract.t: In many standards track documents several words are used to signify the requirements in the specification. These words are often capitalized. This document defines these words as they should be interpreted in IETF documents. This document specifies an Internet Best Current Practices for the Internet Community, and requests discussion and suggestions for improvements.

front.title: Ambiguity of Uppercase vs Lowercase in RFC 2119 Key Words

abstract.t: RFC 2119 specifies common key words that may be used in protocol specifications. This document aims to reduce the ambiguity by clarifying that only UPPERCASE usage of the key words have the defined special meanings.

This document describes version 2.0 of the Certificate Transparency (CT) protocol for publicly logging the existence of Transport Layer Security (TLS) server certificates as they are issued or observed, in a manner that allows anyone to audit certification authority (CA) activity and notice the issuance of suspect certificates as well as to audit the certificate logs themselves. The intent is that eventually clients would refuse to honor certificates that do not appear in a log, effectively forcing CAs to add all issued certificates to the logs.
This document obsoletes RFC 6962. It also specifies a new TLS extension that is used to send various CT log artifacts.
Logs are network services that implement the protocol operations for submissions and queries that are defined in this document.

The Internet Protocol Suite is increasingly used on small devices with severe constraints on power, memory, and processing resources, creating constrained-node networks. This document provides a number of basic terms that have been useful in the standardization work for constrained-node networks.

This document describes Merkle Tree certificates, a new form of X.509 certificates which integrate public logging of the certificate, in the style of Certificate Transparency. The integrated design reduces logging overhead in the face of both shorter-lived certificates and large post-quantum signature algorithms, while still achieving comparable security properties to existing X.509 constructions and Certificate Transparency. Merkle Tree certificates additionally admit an optional size optimization that avoids signatures altogether, at the cost of only applying to up-to-date relying parties and older certificates.

front.title: Adapting Constrained Devices for Post-Quantum Cryptography

abstract.t: This document provides guidance on integrating Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC) into resource-constrained devices, such as IoT nodes and dedicated key-storage hardware. These systems often operate with strict limitations on processing power, RAM, and flash memory, and may even be battery-powered. The document emphasizes the role of hardware security as the basis for secure operations, supporting features such as seed-based key generation to minimize persistent storage, efficient handling of ephemeral keys, and the offloading of cryptographic tasks in low-resource environments. It also explores the implications of PQC on firmware update mechanisms in such constrained systems.

This document specifies a CBOR encoding of X.509 certificates. The resulting certificates are called C509 certificates. The CBOR encoding supports a large subset of RFC 5280 and common certificate profiles, and it is extensible.
Two types of C509 certificates are defined. One type is an invertible CBOR re-encoding of DER-encoded X.509 certificates with the signature field copied from the DER encoding. The other type is identical except that the signature is computed over the CBOR encoding instead of the DER encoding, thereby avoiding the use of ASN.1. Both types of certificates have the same semantics as X.509 while providing comparable size reduction.
This document also specifies CBOR-encoded data structures for certification requests and certification request templates, new COSE headers, as well as a TLS certificate type and a file format for C509. This document updates RFC 6698 by extending the TLSA selectors registry to include C509 certificates.

The Concise Binary Object Representation (CBOR) is a data format whose design goals include the possibility of extremely small code size, fairly small message size, and extensibility without the need for version negotiation. These design goals make it different from earlier binary serializations such as ASN.1 and MessagePack.

This document obsoletes RFC 7049, providing editorial improvements, new details, and errata fixes while keeping full compatibility with the interchange format of RFC 7049. It does not create a new version of the format.

front.title: CBOR Object Signing and Encryption (COSE): Structures and Process

abstract.t: Concise Binary Object Representation (CBOR) is a data format designed for small code size and small message size. There is a need to be able to define basic security services for this data format. This document defines the CBOR Object Signing and Encryption (COSE) protocol. This specification describes how to create and process signatures, message authentication codes, and encryption using CBOR for serialization. This specification additionally describes how to represent cryptographic keys using CBOR.
This document, along with RFC 9053, obsoletes RFC 8152.

This document defines the TLS Trust Anchors extension, a mechanism for a TLS client or server to select a certificate to present based on the peer's trusted certification authorities. It describes certification authorities more succinctly than the TLS Certificate Authorities extension.

front.title: Concise Binary Object Representation (CBOR) Tags for Object Identifiers

abstract.t: The Concise Binary Object Representation (CBOR), defined in RFC 8949, is a data format whose design goals include the possibility of extremely small code size, fairly small message size, and extensibility without the need for version negotiation.
This document defines CBOR tags for object identifiers (OIDs) and is the reference document for the IANA registration of the CBOR tags so defined.

front.title: CBOR Object Signing and Encryption (COSE): Countersignatures

abstract.t: Concise Binary Object Representation (CBOR) is a data format designed for small code size and small message size. CBOR Object Signing and Encryption (COSE) defines a set of security services for CBOR. This document defines a countersignature algorithm along with the needed header parameters and CBOR tags for COSE. This document updates RFC 9052.

front.title: Object Security for Constrained RESTful Environments (OSCORE)

abstract.t: This document defines Object Security for Constrained RESTful Environments (OSCORE), a method for application-layer protection of the Constrained Application Protocol (CoAP), using CBOR Object Signing and Encryption (COSE). OSCORE provides end-to-end protection between endpoints communicating using CoAP or CoAP-mappable HTTP. OSCORE is designed for constrained nodes and networks supporting a range of proxy operations, including translation between different transport protocols.
Although an optional functionality of CoAP, OSCORE alters CoAP options processing and IANA registration. Therefore, this document updates RFC 7252.

front.title: Observing Resources in the Constrained Application Protocol (CoAP)

abstract.t: The Constrained Application Protocol (CoAP) is a RESTful application protocol for constrained nodes and networks. The state of a resource on a CoAP server can change over time. This document specifies a simple protocol extension for CoAP that enables CoAP clients to "observe" resources, i.e., to retrieve a representation of a resource and keep this representation updated by the server over a period of time. The protocol follows a best-effort approach for sending new representations to clients and provides eventual consistency between the state observed by each client and the actual resource state at the server.
